claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6, map safety representations before and during successful jailbreaks in two open-weight aligned models, such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Construct matched triplets consisting of a plainly stated harmful request, a successful jailbreak preserving the same request, and a benign length/topic-matched prompt, using public HarmBench and JailbreakBench behaviors and attacks; verify success with the public HarmBench classifier plus blinded human review of a sample. Cache every attention-head output and residual-stream state. On a discovery split, define each head's safety direction from refused harmful prompts versus benign prompts, then test on held-out behaviors whether jailbreaks selectively reduce projection onto that direction. Separately measure harmful-content decodability from every head and layer using cross-validated linear probes, with attack families held out to prevent wrapper memorization. Predefine 'small subset' as no more than 5% of heads and 'selective suppression' as that subset explaining most of the jailbreak-associated loss of refusal-direction signal after false-discovery correction. Persistence would be supported if successful jailbreaks reduce safety-routing signals in a small subset while harmfulness remains decodable from many other heads at approximately the level seen for unjailbroken harmful prompts; loss of decodability across the network would instead support elimination, while diffuse changes would refute selective suppression. Publicly released, prompt-level activation traces covering the same models and matched conditions could make new inference runs unnecessary, although the analyses would still need to be reproduced.

To address subclaim 5 and strengthen subclaims 3 and 4 causally, intervene on the head subset identified in Experiment 1 using a completely held-out portion of HarmBench and JailbreakBench. For plain harmful prompts that normally elicit refusal, zero, mean-ablate, or remove only the refusal-direction component of those heads during generation, and measure whether outputs change to substantive harmful compliance. For successful jailbreaks, perform the reverse intervention by activation-patching the corresponding head components from the matched refused prompt and test whether refusal is restored. Include equal-sized random-head subsets, activation-norm-matched subsets, heads selected for general language modeling importance, sham hooks, benign prompts, and subset-size dose-response curves. Score refusal, compliance, and harmfulness with the HarmBench classifier, blinded human ratings, and benign utility/perplexity controls; preregister a large causal criterion, such as the selected subset producing a substantially greater compliance change than 95% of matched random subsets without broad degradation. If suppressing the small subset reliably converts refusals to harmful compliance and restoring it reverses jailbreaks, the bypass mechanism and sufficiency claim gain strong support. If only broad ablation works, if random heads work equally well, or if outputs merely become incoherent, the claim is not supported. Public intervention logs containing per-prompt outputs for selected and matched-control heads could substitute for rerunning generation if they include all stated controls.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, freeze the persistent heads and representation locations found in Experiment 1, then evaluate a genuinely label-free direct readout on previously unseen attack families and datasets. Use a preregistered logit-lens score: apply the model's existing layer normalization and unembedding to each selected internal state, compute fixed log-odds for model-tokenized harmful/unsafe versus harmless/safe verbalizers, aggregate across heads with a fixed median or maximum, and use a zero threshold without fitting weights or thresholds. Test on public WildGuardMix, XSTest, HarmBench, and JailbreakBench splits with behavior and attack-family separation. Compare this no-training detector against a supervised linear probe on the same activations, simple output/refusal heuristics, and publicly available dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and WildGuard. Report AUROC, AUPRC, balanced accuracy, calibration, and true-positive rate at fixed 1% and 5% false-positive rates, including benign hard negatives and successful jailbreaks; define competitiveness in advance with a noninferiority margin, for example no more than three percentage points below the best dedicated model on macro-averaged AUROC and fixed-FPR recall. Competitive performance from the frozen zero-training score would support direct readout without additional training; success only after fitting a probe would show that representations persist but refute the no-additional-training claim; poor performance from both would undermine detector feasibility. A public benchmark submission containing frozen readout code, untouched test predictions, and scores against the same baselines could remove the need to repeat this evaluation.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-request, layer- and component-resolved comparison that can distinguish residual safety-related signal from complete erasure during successful attacks.
reference_coverage.rationale: The triplets preserve the harmful request while varying attack status, and the experiment caches and analyzes every head and layer. It measures both the attack-associated reduction in a refusal-direction projection and whether harmful content remains decodable elsewhere, directly testing persistence versus elimination.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A sufficiently varied paired evaluation set containing harmful requests with verified refusal baselines and successful attack variants that preserve the underlying request, so attack effects can be isolated from prompt-content differences.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 0 explicitly constructs matched harmful, successful-jailbreak, and benign triplets and verifies outcomes; Experiment 1 adds held-out harmful behaviors and attack datasets. The proposed set therefore supplies the paired conditions needed for within-request comparisons without requiring the reference set's exact yield or size.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level scoring and selection procedure that identifies a small attack-sensitive subset relative to the remaining components, with an explicit statistical rule limiting false discoveries and reducing dependence on an arbitrary cutoff.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 defines component safety directions on a discovery split, evaluates head-specific loss of refusal signal on held-out behaviors, and predefines the small-subset and selective-suppression criteria with false-discovery correction. Experiment 1 uses dose-response and matched controls to validate the selected subset, providing the required selection and validation by a different but comparably discriminating route.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal, dose-dependent intervention on the candidate head subset, with matched random or otherwise controlled subsets and substantive-compliance outcomes, that can show the subset itself converts a normally refused harmful request into compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed intervention removes or ablates only the selected head components, includes random, norm-matched, importance-matched, sham, benign, and subset-size controls, and scores refusal, harmful compliance, and coherence. It also includes the complementary restoration intervention, so it tests sufficiency at least as directly as the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the non-target heads themselves retain and carry a harmful-content signal during successful attacks, rather than the apparent persistence being only a property of the selected suppressible subset.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures harmful-content decodability from every head and layer and would show whether many other heads still encode the harmful content during successful attacks. However, it does not suppress the persistent/non-target head population and measure the resulting signal change, so it leaves ambiguous whether those heads are a causal source of the persistent signal rather than merely correlated or redundant carriers.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 4 uses a perturbation of the other head population to test whether that population carries the persistent signal.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 probes decodability in those representations but does not perturb that population.
[3] Persistent decodability can coexist with a representation that is redundant, correlated, or not causally responsible for the measured signal.
[4] Proposed experiment 1 intervenes on the selected suppressible subset, not on the other persistent heads.
[5] Therefore the team would learn that harmful content remains decodable in other heads, but would fail to learn whether those heads causally supply the persistent signal.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token- or otherwise input-partitioned evidence that the two head populations respond similarly to the original harmful request while differing specifically in their handling of attack-template material, thereby separating selective bypass from different harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The matched same-request design and held-out attack-family evaluation in proposed experiment 0 bear on whether the result is just memorization of a particular wrapper. But the experiment does not attribute activations to harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens or directly compare the two populations on those contributions, so the rival sensitivity explanation remains viable.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 isolates contributions from harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens to distinguish bypass from differential harmful-content sensitivity.

[2] Proposed experiment 0 holds the underlying request matched and holds out attack families, which tests generalization beyond particular wrappers but only at an aggregate representation/decodability level.
[3] Aggregate decodability does not reveal whether a head-type difference came from harmful-request content, attack-template content, or their changed context and positions.
[4] No proposed experiment performs the needed input-partitioned attribution or an equivalent controlled token contribution comparison.
[5] Therefore the team would fail to decisively distinguish selective attack-template handling from a difference in sensitivity to harmful content.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally held-out, training-free detector evaluation that tests transfer across unseen harmful-content conditions and quantitatively compares the direct readout with the model's own behavior and dedicated safety systems.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 2 specifies a frozen zero-training readout, separates behaviors and attack families, evaluates on multiple held-out benchmarks including successful jailbreaks and hard benign negatives, and compares quantitative performance with refusal heuristics, a trained probe, and several dedicated safety models. The reference's particular benchmark count and model roster are not binding requirements of the claim.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests every stated subclaim: persistence versus elimination, selective localization, causal conversion to compliance, continued harmful-content decodability, and a no-training detector competitive with dedicated safety models. It leaves two mechanistic evidential gaps relative to the reference account: the persistent non-target signal is not tested by suppressing those heads, and the head effects are not decomposed into harmful-request versus jailbreak-template token contributions. Thus the central claim could be strongly evaluated, but the strongest causal and rival-explanation interpretation would remain incomplete.
